overview: The atlas paints Hainan as one separate “state” from about 700 to 1492. Its neat island outline barely changes, even while the nearby mainland switches from Tang to Song, Yuan and Ming. Real history was less tidy. Imperial governments created counties, registered households, collected taxes, sent officials and exiled famous critics, but their reach varied sharply between ports, farming districts and the forested central mountains. Communities now grouped under names such as Li or Hlai were diverse; the modern ethnic label, language map and Latin-based writing system cannot simply be carried backward. Sediment cores record intensified land use and migration, while chronicles, gazetteers, archaeology and living traditions each reveal different slices of life. Families farmed rice and yams, fished, gathered forest products, wove cotton, traded incense and maintained waterworks. Women’s textile knowledge became famous, although individual medieval makers are rarely named. Children learned at home and work; some entered schools that spread unevenly. Storms, malaria-like fevers, exile, taxation and warfare made island life difficult. A 1489 canal shows impressive cooperation. Toilets are harder: no securely excavated island-wide medieval latrine lets us describe everybody’s bathroom. The target vanishes in 1492 because the atlas changes categories; Hainan’s peoples and Ming administration continued.

periods.title: Tang counties, mediated rule and dangerous sea crossings
periods.summary: The atlas begins an island-wide state, but Tang administration relied on counties, local intermediaries and uneven enforcement. Jianzhen’s 748 landing belongs to a maritime and Buddhist story; penal exile shows that travel south could also be coerced and frightening.

periods.title: Tang migration, roads and incomplete interior control
periods.summary: The exact polygon stays fixed. Museum and sediment evidence point to migration and stronger land use, while research on Tang governance still finds loose rule and resistance. Coast, county seat and mountain community cannot be collapsed into one political experience.

periods.title: Dynastic fragmentation beyond a deceptively stable island color
periods.summary: The atlas keeps both Hainan and its mainland Tang seam unchanged until 1000, smoothing over the Five Dynasties and Southern Han era. The period is best presented as documentary uncertainty and changing regional rule, not a surviving sovereign Hainan state.

periods.title: Song administration, migration, schools and maritime traffic
periods.summary: The mainland seam becomes Song while Hainan retains its separate color. Song-era sources describe expanded administration, farming, education and transit trade, but access and control often remained uneven in practice, particularly toward the central interior.

periods.title: Su Shi’s Danzhou exile and one unusually visible household
periods.summary: Su Shi lived in exile at Danzhou from 1097 until his pardon in 1100. His writings illuminate elite learning, illness and self-care more vividly than most lives, so this brief subdivision is useful without making one celebrated scholar representative of Hainan.

periods.title: Song institutions grow while island societies stay plural
periods.summary: The map returns to its original component hash and keeps the mainland Song seam. Schools, examination culture, trade and migration expanded, but mountain and coastal communities retained distinct languages, skills and relationships with officials in practice.

periods.title: Late Song cotton, trade and localized waterworks
periods.summary: The last Song interval includes growing records of Hainan cotton goods, transit routes and irrigation. Huang Daopo traditions preserve cross-cultural craft memory, but later stories need testing against texts, tools and dates rather than turning one woman into a lone inventor.

periods.title: Yuan rule begins across an unchanged island polygon
periods.summary: The mainland seam switches to Yuan and the target geometry drifts by tiny coordinate fractions. Yuan authorities increased registration, taxes and labor demands, yet divided jurisdictions and resistance prevented uniform control of every community in practice.

periods.title: Yuan administration, migration and continuing regional differences
periods.summary: The same atlas component persists. Written records describe administration and exchange, while genetic and linguistic studies offer only cautious evidence about deeper population history. Neither can turn diverse medieval islanders into one timeless ethnic block.

periods.title: Ming Qiongzhou, canals, coercion and an editorial ending
periods.summary: The target remains separate even as Yuan and Ming overlap on tested mainland points. Ming officials expanded registration, schools and waterworks amid repeated Li resistance. The id disappears at 1492 without a successor owner, although Ming administration and island communities continued.

sections.title: Read the map before believing its color

items.text: The live record is a generated state layer called Hainan, covering nine consecutive intervals from 700 to 1492. It currently has only an imported modern summary. That is an editorial object to investigate, not proof that one island kingdom, ethnicity or government lasted unchanged for nearly eight centuries.

Every target snapshot uses one 26-position Polygon around the island. Three component hashes differ only through minute coordinate drift, not meaningful expansion. A few shoreline test points fall outside the simplified coast while nearby inland points remain inside, demonstrating cartographic simplification rather than historical exclusion.

Xuwen and Beihai across the strait belong to Tang, then Song, then Yuan; in 1400 both Yuan and Ming layers claim them. Hainan nonetheless keeps its separate target color. This seam exposes the atlas taxonomy: neighboring dynasties change while the island is artificially held apart.

Chronicles and gazetteers name officials, exiles, taxes, schools and revolts; archaeology and sediment cores reveal objects and land use; later traditions preserve skills. Each source has blind spots. Famous men dominate texts, cores blur individual events, and a living practice cannot be assigned an eighth-century birthday without proof.

“Li,” “Hlai,” Han migrant and islander are not interchangeable timeless boxes. Modern ethnography and state classification helped stabilize today’s Li category; Hlai varieties also differ. Population genetics can model ancestry among sampled people, but it cannot label a medieval pot, household or rebel by itself.

sections.title: Mountains, rivers, forests and stormy coasts

items.text: Hainan rises toward a mountainous center, and major rivers flow outward toward different coasts. That terrain created many local travel and farming worlds rather than one flat island landscape. River valleys could support fields and movement, while steep forested country complicated official journeys and military control.

A tropical monsoon brings heavy rain, but not evenly: eastern slopes receive more, western districts can be drier, and typhoons, droughts or unusual cold can damage crops. People needed flexible planting, storage and repair routines; a green island was never automatically an easy pantry.

Offshore sediment cores preserve pollen, chemical indicators and erosion signals. Researchers connect stronger human impacts with migration in the Sui to Tang and especially Song periods. Core dates and source areas have uncertainties, so the evidence supports broad land-use intensification rather than a headcount for any one village.

At Shuangchi Maar, pollen, charcoal and radiocarbon dates reveal long environmental histories. Such archives help distinguish climate shifts, burning and vegetation change, but they do not identify who lit a fire or why. Environmental science adds scale while written and archaeological evidence supply more local context.

Central rainforest supported plants, animals, gathering, hunting and settlement while also sheltering communities beyond easy county supervision. UNESCO’s nomination links ecology with long Li continuity, but its modern heritage boundaries and ethnic language cannot simply be laid over every medieval century.

sections.title: Officials, counties and power that faded with distance

items.text: Tang rulers established or reorganized counties but often worked through the influential Feng-Xian family and other local intermediaries. Scholarship describes elements of loose or indirect administration and episodes of resistance. A county name on paper did not guarantee an official could command every mountain settlement.

The 900 to 1000 interval is unusually deceptive: the map leaves the Tang seam and island polygon unchanged while regimes around the region fractured and Southern Han power arose. The responsible card marks this as a source-and-map mismatch instead of inventing an independent Hainan dynasty to fill the color.

Song government expanded administrative divisions and special arrangements for interior communities, while migration and commerce increased. Research on central Hainan still finds sharp differences in reach and interaction. Governance was negotiated through county seats, markets and local leaders rather than broadcast equally across the island.

Yuan authorities pursued household registration, taxes and corvée, but Hainan remained divided among institutions and control was unstable. Registration itself could provoke evasion or resistance. A tax roll reveals what officials sought to count; it never captures everybody who moved, hid or lived beyond routine collection.

Ming Qiongzhou Prefecture dates from 1369 in the museum chronology. Officials promoted farming and schools while expanding registration, yet repeated resistance and suppression show the coercive side of state-building. Development language in official sources must be read beside the people whose labor and land were being reorganized.

sections.title: Movement, exile, belief and many kinds of neighbor

items.text: The Buddhist monk Jianzhen landed near Yazhou in 748 after a failed Japan voyage and stayed before continuing. His story places Hainan inside sea routes and religious networks. Later memorial sites celebrate him, so historians separate the voyage tradition from buildings or ceremonies created much later.

Exile was forced movement, not an adventurous holiday. Tang legal history describes long journeys, labor, loss of status and uncertain return. Hainan’s distance made it useful to governments as punishment. Families, servants and local hosts could bear costs that an exiled official’s elegant poem rarely records.

Su Shi’s 1097 to 1100 Danzhou exile is exceptionally well documented. He wrote, taught and managed illness while depending on local relationships. His voice helps animate one place and three years, but its survival reflects male elite literacy; thousands of neighbors left no comparable diary or collected works.

Migration increased cultivated land, markets and cultural contact, particularly in the Song period. Newcomers did not arrive on an empty island, and “migration” covers officials, soldiers, farmers, merchants, family members and forced travelers. Contact could bring exchange, marriage, competition, disease and conflict in different combinations.

Ports connected Buddhists, merchants, sailors and other travelers with mainland China and the wider sea. Evidence for particular Muslim communities or foreign traders is uneven and later traditions may compress centuries. It is safer to describe documented maritime diversity than assign every visiting cargo a permanent neighborhood.

sections.title: Rice, yams, fish, forest foods and shared water

items.text: Farmers grew crops suited to wet lowlands and drier or sloping ground. Rice mattered, while local historical synthesis also finds yams in Song and Yuan writing. Diet still varied by ecology, season and wealth; one list of crops cannot tell us the contents of every family bowl.

Fishing linked shore, estuary and river communities, while gathering and hunting used forest knowledge. Later records describe organized Li hunts, but projecting their exact rules backward would be unsafe. Archaeological bones, tools and settlement context are needed to identify which species were eaten at a particular site.

Betel nut became a valued social and medicinal product in southern China. Historical medical research traces changing claims about its effects, including Song discussion. Chewing, trading and prescribing are different activities, and old medical authority does not prove that every remedy was effective or harmless.

Forest products, especially aromatic goods such as incense, entered exchange networks connecting interior collectors, local brokers and ports. Those chains created opportunity and inequality. A fragrant object in an elite market could begin with difficult, poorly recorded labor far from the official who described its price.

Waterworks required surveying, digging, gates, cleaning and agreements about turns. A local synthesis records Song works and a canal built in 1489. That late-Ming project is a real achievement inside the interval: less flashy than a palace, but potentially more useful when children, fields and animals needed water.

sections.title: Cotton, tools, markets and sea-spanning exchange

items.text: Song and Yuan texts record Hainan cotton and mixed-fiber textiles. Production joined plant cultivation, cleaning, spinning, dyeing, weaving and finishing, often across several hands. A finished bolt embodies practiced knowledge and time; it should not be reduced to a single “invention moment” in a famous biography.

Traditions connect Huang Daopo, a late-Song woman, with learning cotton techniques from Li communities before transforming production near Shanghai. Scholars debate details and later embellishment. The responsible lesson is cross-cultural technical exchange and women’s expertise, not a fairy tale in which one genius invents weaving alone.

UNESCO’s living-heritage record documents spinning, plant dyeing, weaving and embroidery taught especially from mothers to daughters. This is valuable continuity evidence and a clue to embodied learning. It does not make every modern pattern, tool or gender arrangement a securely dated feature of 700 to 1492.

Hainan functioned as a stopping and exchange zone on regional sea routes, especially under the Song. Cargo studies show official, merchant and small-scale networks could coexist. Most islanders were not ocean captains, yet farmers, packers, porters, boat repairers and food sellers helped make voyages possible.

Coins and ceramics recovered offshore can date traffic and commercial connections, but findspots near reefs may lie outside this exact island polygon and shipwreck cargoes may have been merely passing. Maritime archaeology is powerful precisely when location, deposition, corrosion and route alternatives remain explicit.

sections.title: Homes, clothes, work, music and play

items.text: County towns such as Yazhou developed walls, streets, offices, temples, markets and homes over many rebuilding phases. The surviving townscape mixes Song beginnings with later Ming and modern fabric. A present wall is evidence for urban memory, not an untouched backdrop for an eleventh-century street scene.

Boat-shaped houses in some Hainan communities used forms adapted to climate and available materials, but surviving examples and recent architectural studies are later. They offer comparative questions about ventilation, rain and shared space; they do not justify placing every medieval Hlai-speaking family in an identical house.

Clothing could use cotton and other fibers, shaped by work, climate, status and local fashion. Living Li textile traditions preserve extraordinary color and pattern knowledge, while medieval texts emphasize goods more often than wardrobes. The card therefore shows craft without inventing one island costume for eight centuries.

Daily labor included farming, water repair, fishing, gathering, childcare, cooking, weaving, carrying goods, sailing, clerical work and military service. Who performed a task varied by place, age, gender, wealth and compulsion. Official histories rarely count the sore backs behind a canal or cargo list.

Museum exhibits and today’s Yazhou song tradition preserve instruments, games, dance and oral performance, giving children an honest reminder that work was not the whole day. Exact medieval tunes and rules are not securely recoverable. We can say people made music and jokes without writing fake lyrics for them.

sections.title: Families, women, children and unequal chances to learn

items.text: Households could include couples, children, elders, other kin, servants or dependents, but composition differed by community and status. Migration and exile separated some families and joined others. Genealogies preserve prominent lines far better than ordinary households, so no single “Hainan family” fits the interval.

Women’s textile knowledge is visible through both historical traditions and living practice, yet medieval women are seldom named individually. Huang Daopo’s exceptional fame should direct attention toward many teachers and makers, not erase them. Women also farmed, traded, managed homes and cared for people in varied arrangements.

Children learned speech, manners, food gathering, craft and work by watching, helping and practicing with relatives and neighbors. Mother-to-daughter textile teaching is documented in living heritage, not directly for every medieval village. Archaeology rarely records the patient corrections, teasing and repeated mistakes of apprenticeship.

Song officials and local advocates expanded schools, examinations and ritual education, but provision and access were uneven. Formal study favored families with time, connections and literacy; mountain distance mattered. A school’s existence does not mean every boy attended, and absence from rosters does not mean girls learned nothing.

Su Shi is remembered as a teacher in Danzhou, offering a vivid example of learned exchange during exile. He represents Classical Chinese literary culture, not all island childhood. Children in fishing, farming, craft and forest communities learned valuable knowledge that official examination records were not designed to recognize.

sections.title: Illness, care, drinking water and the toilet evidence gap

items.text: Hainan’s heat, rain, insects, storms and difficult travel shaped health risks. Older writers often portrayed the far south as dangerously unhealthy, sometimes exaggerating to dramatize exile. Illness was real, but hostile literary stereotypes are not clinical surveys and should not make island residents seem naturally sickly.

Historical research dates stronger Chinese medical institutions on Hainan to the Song and records Ming medical offices. Wider Song government medicine included texts, pharmacies and official programs, but island access was uneven. Most care still began with household food, rest, observation and locally known plants.

Su Shi’s writings describe diet, rest and strategies for enduring illness during exile. They make self-care unusually personal, yet he was a literate official with distinctive resources and beliefs. His regimen should appear as one documented case rather than “what Hainan people did” when sick.

Rivers, springs, wells, rain storage and canals could supply households and fields, but water had to be carried and protected from contamination. The sources document waterways and irrigation better than drinking practices. Children likely helped with water work, though exact chores require local household evidence.

No cited excavation securely supplies an island-wide medieval toilet design for 700 to 1492. People certainly managed urine, feces, wash water and rubbish, but arrangements varied by town, village and field. The scientifically honest bathroom fact is the gap itself: never turn a later house drain into everybody’s toilet.

sections.title: Conflict, achievements, one written voice and continuity

items.text: Resistance labeled “Li rebellions” in Ming records arose from taxation, registration, land pressure, abuses and local political struggles, followed by military suppression. Official labels can flatten different communities and motives. Violence affected food, homes and families, not merely the careers of commanders listed in chronicles.

Exile, taxation and corvée were also forms of coercion. A road, field or office might look like administrative progress while demanding forced travel or labor from particular people. Reading achievements honestly means asking who chose, who paid, who benefited and whose objections survived only as “disorder.”

Island achievements accumulated across communities: irrigation and canals, cotton skill, ports and navigation, schools, local ecological knowledge, farming, music and rebuilding after storms. The best history does not award them all to a dynasty or modern ethnicity; cooperation and exchange often outlasted official regimes.

Localized written sample, June 1100: 九死南荒吾不恨，茲遊奇絕冠平生。 Jiǔ sǐ nánhuāng wú bù hèn; zī yóu qíjué guàn píngshēng. “Even nine deaths in the southern wilds would bring no regret; this wondrous journey surpasses all my life.” It is Su Shi’s Classical Chinese voice after Danzhou exile, not a Hlai or island-wide voice.

No in-period Hlai text is securely attributable: the current Latin-based orthography dates to 1957, so borrowing it would fake a medieval sample. At 1492 the atlas id simply disappears and leaves tested island points unowned. Ming administration, Hlai-speaking communities and other island lives continued beyond the map category.

ending.text: The exact Hainan target disappears at 1492, and audited points at Danzhou, Wuzhishan, Sanya and elsewhere gain no automatic successor owner in that snapshot. This is an atlas taxonomy boundary rather than a conquest, migration or extinction. Hainan remained under Ming institutions of uneven reach, while Hlai-speaking communities, migrant families, ports, farms, crafts and island exchange continued and changed beyond this card.
